chapters.title: Getting started
chapters.description: Install, import, develop, and export. For a first session, use a color negative with normal exposure.
chapters.body:
Install

Download NextFrame, install it, and open the app. If your system asks for access to a photo folder, choose the folder you want to process.

Workspace

The library is where you import and organize frames. Click Import Folder to add a folder, or Add Frames to choose files. Select a photo and click Develop to start editing.

In Develop, the filmstrip is on the left, the preview is in the center, and the adjustment panels are on the right. Click a thumbnail to switch photos. While a mask is selected, panel settings apply to that mask. Back on the global adjustments, they apply to the whole photo.

Import and process a negative

  1. Open Settings → Processing Preferences and turn on Auto Process.
  2. Under Auto Crop, choose Keep Base or Remove Base.
  3. Import the photos and wait until processing finishes.
  4. Open Develop. Press F to check the crop, and V to show the range and sample marks.
  5. Check orientation, edges, and color. To change them, see Automatic RAW mode and Color.
  6. Press ⌘ S to open export. Choose the photos, format, size, and destination, then export.

Slides are imported as the original image, with negative inversion off. See Slides and black-and-white negatives.

Check the export

Open the destination folder and confirm the count and file names. Check orientation, size, and color in the actual files. For ordinary web sharing, choose SDR, JPEG, and sRGB.

This guide refers to NextFrame 2.62. Shortcuts are shown for macOS. On Windows, use the matching Ctrl combination.

Follow the beginner tips

Enable Beginner mode at startup. After import, press V to inspect the base sample and exposure range. Complete the action or choose Skip to dismiss its tip. Beginner mode switches off when you finish all the tips. Turn it on again under Processing Preferences → Habits to start from the first tip. Open Guide next to Directories in the upper-left corner of the home screen for more help.

chapters.title: Choose a workflow
chapters.description: Pick a path from the film type.
chapters.body:
Which path

Source Use
A single color negative copied with a camera Automatic RAW mode
A TIFF, FFF, or DNG that contains several frames Strip scans and frame splitting
A strip you want to grade frame by frame, then crop Absolute masks
Slide film Original-image path
Black-and-white negative Invert, then turn on grayscale output if you want it

File format and film type are separate questions. A DNG might be one copied frame or a whole strip. A TIFF might contain only one photo.

Film base

Keep Base retains edge codes and sprocket holes. Remove Base keeps only the picture. Either way, crop away the light panel, scanner bed, and continuous white border outside the film. Sprocket holes filled white inside the base can stay.

Format of a strip scan

Confirm half-frame, 135, 6×6, 6×7, or XPAN, then count the actual frames. After automatic detection, check the first frame, the last frame, and frames in between. If the spacing varies, or the strip mixes formats, adjust the crop boxes separately.

chapters.title: How to automatically convert a full roll of RAW film negatives without Lightroom
chapters.description: Turn on Auto Process in NextFrame and import a folder of camera-scanned RAW negatives. NextFrame detects, crops, inverts, and color-corrects each exposure using your preset. Review representative frames, adjust any exceptions, and batch export the positives in the same desktop app.
chapters.body:
If one file contains a row of frames, start with splitting a film strip scan.

From a roll of negatives to individual positives

Put the camera captures from one roll in one folder, with one exposure per RAW file. Set the processing preferences below, then import the folder into the library. Once processing finishes, review a typical frame, a dark one, and a bright one. Press V to check the base sample and exposure range. Press A to redraw a range that includes the next exposure. Select the frames you want, check their count in the export window, and export them together.

Both views come from the same Sony α7R III capture. Use the tree trunk and sprocket holes to match the two images. Check that the analysis rectangle excludes adjacent exposures before judging detail in grass and shade. See the color science of film negative conversion for how the base sample affects color.

Set the default

  1. Open Settings → Processing Preferences, or press ⌘ Shift ,.
  2. Turn on Auto Process. Under Auto Crop, choose Keep Base or Remove Base. Choose Straighten if you only need the angle corrected.
  3. Set automatic Dmin, automatic straightening, sprocket fill, automatic tone, and temperature and tint as needed.
  4. Choose the default color mode. Turn on cloud color-cast correction if you want it, and keep a network connection available.
  5. Import the RAW files and wait until processing finishes.

Processing preferences apply to newly imported photos and to photos after a reset. They do not rewrite an edit that is already open. Strip scans do not use the single-RAW automatic path.

Run it again

In Develop, select the photo, hold A to open the dial, and choose Auto. This recalculates inversion and related settings. To keep the hand adjustments you already made, press ⌘ D first and work on a virtual copy.

Hold D to choose the automatic crop: keep the base, remove the base, or straighten. A short press of D toggles between the automatic crop and no crop. Hold S to choose Vivid, Natural, or Original tone.

Check the crop and the range

Press F to crop. Check that the light panel, film holder, or a neighboring frame is not left in the edges. Drag an edge to change it, press Enter to confirm, or Esc to discard this change.

Press V to show the marks. Check that the sample point sits on clean, unexposed film base and that the exposure rectangle covers the picture. If the rectangle includes sprocket holes, the holder, or the next frame, press A to redraw it. Hold A to pick a range preset.

Here the cyan rectangle excludes the next frame, while the yellow circle lies close to the edge lettering. Try sampling a clear patch away from the letters and compare the whole positive. If there is no clear base, try the darkest reliable area in the positive. If the sample does not help, clear it. See Inversion and sampling.

Check the sprockets

With the base kept, press G to toggle sprocket fill, and hold G to adjust the threshold. Zoom in and look for holes that were missed. Also confirm that dark parts of the picture and the edge codes were not filled white. The final crop should not keep the continuous white border outside the film.

Color and export

If the automatic result looks right, export it. If the whole frame has a cast, check the exposure range and film-base sample first. If neutral objects still look tinted, try the DCMY eyedropper, then fine-tune white balance as needed. See Color. Press ⌘ S to open export (Ctrl S on Windows).

chapters.title: How to split a film strip scan into individual frames
chapters.description: When one FFF, TIFF, or DNG scan contains several exposures, NextFrame can create a cropped copy for each frame. Use automatic splitting on supported originals, or press F to crop the strip by hand. Export the copies to save each frame as its own image file.
chapters.body:
Flextight X5 and FFF workflow: choosing the original scan

For a Hasselblad Flextight X5 workflow, start with the original 3F scan. The worked example uses 1 002.tiff, a TIFF with a Flextight input profile that NextFrame reads as Scan3F. Viewed horizontally, it contains two strips of six exposures each. Select the full scan to begin splitting.

Automatic FFF split

  1. Import the scan and select the whole strip in the library.
  2. For a supported original, choose “Process FFF/DNG automatically” from its context menu or click Auto split. For example, when working with a Hasselblad Flextight X5 strip, select the original FFF scan.
  3. Under Film Format, choose half-frame, 135, 6×6, or 6×7.
  4. Check the detected strip count and total frames, then confirm to create the cropped copies.
  5. If you are asked to realign and rebalance color, choose what you need. Skip it when the color is already where you want it.
  6. Check the edges, orientation, and color of each copy, then export.

Use a manual crop for XPAN and for scans that were not detected reliably. Automatic splitting creates separate editable copies. Those copies still have to be saved as image files through the export window.

Check the frame boundaries. The overlay below plots the 12 saved crop rectangles on the original scan, numbered in reading order. Look at the gap between 03 and 04. Each rectangle should end inside its own exposure. If a crop includes the neighboring exposure, open that copy, press F, adjust its edge, and confirm.

Check orientation and a single result. This contact sheet uses the developed previews of all 12 copies from the same scan. Frames 01 and 02 are upright portraits and 03 is a landscape. Open 03 and check the horizon, driftwood, and left and right edges for any part of the next frame.

Crop a strip by hand

  1. After import, count the strips and the frames on each strip. Confirm orientation and format.
  2. Press A and draw the useful area inside one strip. If you need a Dmin sample, press Q on clean base or in the gap between frames.
  3. Press F to crop, and choose Strip.
  4. Set the number of groups, frames per group, and spacing. Adjust the overall box, the offset between groups, and the angle.
  5. Line up the first frame and the last frame, then check the frames in between. A crop box must not cross into the next picture.
  6. Confirm the crop and check the result count in the filmstrip.

If frame count, spacing, or format is inconsistent inside one file, work in groups. Crop frame by frame when you have to.

Inversion after the split

Select the split results. Hold A and choose Exposure Range 90% as a common starting point. That setting keeps 90% of the width and 90% of the height. Check each frame for interfering color. Sky, snow, and similar pictures can use their own range.

Export

For this scan, select the 12 cropped copies and open export (⌘ S on macOS or Ctrl S on Windows). Check that the selection count is 12. For web sharing, choose JPEG, SDR, and sRGB, select the destination, and start the export. Check the output folder for 12 individual images and open frame 03 to compare it with the driftwood preview above. See batch export settings.

chapters.title: Absolute masks on a strip
chapters.description: Absolute masks invert and adjust each frame on the same strip scan, then split the strip once at the end.
chapters.body:
Add masks

  1. Set a first exposure range for the whole strip, and sample Dmin if you need it.
  2. In the mask panel, add a Rectangle and choose Absolute.
  3. Place the rectangle on one frame. Make a mask for each other frame. Keep the size the same when the format is the same.
  4. Move them so the masks do not overlap. For the first setup, use no feather and do not invert the mask.

Adjust each frame

Select the mask you want to change, then edit inversion, exposure, and color. To share a range step, select several masks and choose Exposure Range 90%, then check each frame.

An absolute mask can invert on its own. A relative mask adjusts a local area on top of the image you already have. Watch whether the right-hand panel is acting on the mask or on the whole photo.

Crop and export

Press F for the strip crop, line every crop box up with a frame, confirm, and check each copy. Color and sample range should match before and after the split. When they do, select the results and open export.

Crop boxes are covered in Strip scans. Color is covered in Color.

chapters.title: Slides and black-and-white negatives
chapters.description: Slides use the original-image path. Black-and-white negatives are inverted, then adjusted for gray and tone.
chapters.body:
Slides

  1. Import as the original image and confirm that negative inversion is off. Press C to toggle inversion.
  2. P automatic color correction is on by default, with levels stretch at 1. If the cloud service is unavailable, adjust by hand first.
  3. Press F to check the crop and V to check the range.
  4. Adjust exposure, white balance, and curves, and compare the picture with automatic color correction on and off.
  5. Press ⌘ S to export.

If import preferences turn inversion on directly, check a slide after import and turn inversion off.

Black-and-white negatives

Import and invert them as negatives. After the crop and analysis range look right, press B to turn on grayscale. Use the D waveform, tone controls, and curves for the light-to-dark relationship. For a tinted black-and-white look, turn grayscale off and use color grading.

Zoom in on highlights and shadows, then add sharpening, glow, and grain if you want them.

chapters.title: Density inversion and sampling
chapters.description: The inversion panel controls a negative’s brightness and color through a density-domain conversion and the DCMY settings. Exposure range, Dmin, and Dmax set the analysis area and the reference points.
chapters.body:
For the optical density equation and a real camera-scan example, see the color science of film negative conversion.

Density-domain inversion

Film density and transmitted light are related logarithmically. Density-domain inversion works in that relationship, then uses channel baseline, gain, and tone to produce a positive. The controls are not the same as a simple RGB invert.

Press C to toggle inversion. Press S for automatic alignment. Manual DCMY adjustments are in Color.

Exposure range

The exposure range decides which areas are analyzed. It does not change the export boundary.

  • Press A, then drag on the picture to draw the analysis area.
  • Hold A to choose a preset ratio, or choose Auto to process again.
  • Press V to show or hide the range marks.

Keep the exposure range inside the picture, clear of the film holder, sprocket holes, neighboring frames, and large areas of distracting color.

If the range looks right but the positive still has a color cast, check two things.

  1. Are there bright colors inside the range? A few brightly colored lights can influence the analysis even in an otherwise neutral scene. Look for vivid red or yellow lights, especially where a highlight is complementary in color to its surroundings. Redraw the range to leave those lights outside it, then compare the positives to see whether the cast is weaker.
  2. Is the scene nearly a single color? A sky, clouds, or a snow-covered mountain may offer no reliable black point. Try including a small patch of clean film base in the exposure range, then compare the result.

Press V to show the exposure range and sample marks. The picture above is from the current Develop workspace: the range sits inside the picture and avoids sprocket holes and edge codes.

Dmin

Press Q for Dmin and click clean film base. The narrow black edge around the frame, and the gap between frames, are usually usable. Avoid printed codes, holes, and the scanner bed.

If there is no clear base, try the darkest reliable area in the inverted positive. That means a dark area in the positive, not the darkest part of the negative original. Compare color, fog, and contrast after sampling. If it gets worse, click Clear next to Dmin, or undo.

Dmin can be left unset. You do not have to find a sample on every photo.

Dmax

Hold Q and choose Dmax. Sample the brightest neutral highlight in the positive that has not clipped, such as a white wall, white clothing, or a white cloud. Avoid colored lights and colored reflections.

Try Dmax after range, white balance, and cast strength have not improved the picture.

Sample position and crop

A sample can sit outside the final crop, but it should be the same piece of film under the same light. Sample first, then crop away the outer area you do not want. Even when you keep the base, remove the continuous white border outside the film.

chapters.title: The color science of film negative conversion
chapters.description: A film scanner or camera measures light passing through a negative. Optical density expresses how strongly the film attenuates that light. In NextFrame, the film base and exposure range provide references for converting those measurements into a positive. You can then adjust tone and color separately.
chapters.body:
From transmitted light to density

Transmittance, T, is the fraction of incident light that passes through the film. Optical density is D = −log₁₀(T). A patch transmitting 10% of the light has density 1.0. At 1% it has density 2.0. A tenfold change in transmitted light is one step on this scale. This is a physical relationship for linear light measurements. An RGB number from a display JPEG already includes tone encoding.

For a worked introduction to transmittance and density, see Kodak’s Basic Photographic Sensitometry Workbook.

Read the film base before judging color

An unexposed, developed margin on a color negative still has density and often looks orange. It transmits different amounts of red, green, and blue light. Sampling clean base gives the conversion a reference for those channel differences. A sprocket hole lets light through without passing through film. A printed edge code adds density of its own.

In this camera scan, follow the top edge. There is film between the holes and around the lettering. Press V to check where the Dmin point landed. If it falls in a hole or on a letter, use Q to sample a clear patch of base. Keep the exposure rectangle inside the photograph. Press A if it needs redrawing. See inversion and sampling for Dmax and difficult frames.

Separate exposure from a color cast

The D control adjusts the overall density baseline and gain. C, M, and Y affect the red, green, and blue channels respectively. The left end of each waveform controls its baseline and the right end its gain. A gray shadow that looks green and a white highlight that looks green can need different adjustments.

Start with the automatically converted frame. If a subject you know to be neutral has a cast, first check the sample and analysis area. Try the DCMY eyedropper on that neutral subject and inspect both shadows and highlights. Fine-tune white balance if necessary. The grass in the example is a poor neutral reference. The pair shows how one real frame was interpreted. For an ordinary roll, compare skin, neutral objects and shadow detail across nearby frames while preserving the color of the original light.

To use this workflow on your own roll, follow automatic RAW negative conversion.

chapters.title: Color
chapters.description: Check the analysis range first, then white balance and color cast. If the automatic result looks right, do not rebalance it.
chapters.body:
Analysis range

Press V to show the marks. Check whether the exposure range includes sprocket holes, the holder, a neighboring frame, or a large area of interfering color. Shrink the range or draw it again if it does. For sky, cloud, or snow with no black point, try including a little film base.

White balance and cast strength

Press T to apply automatic temperature and tint. If those settings already have adjustments, this key resets them. On a photo you have edited by hand, make a virtual copy first, then compare automatic, reset, and manual results. Press W for the white-balance eyedropper, or adjust global, shadows, midtones, and highlights separately in the white-balance panel.

In the inversion panel, lower Color Cast Strength and compare the current value, a lower value, and 0. A lower strength suits a photo where automatic correction went too far. Press P to toggle cast correction. Calling cloud correction again needs a network connection.

Sunset, stage light, and warm indoor light should keep an appropriate amount of the light that was there. The goal is not a completely neutral picture.

Dmin and Dmax

If fog or a cast remains, check that Dmin landed on the film base. Clear it and sample again if needed. When the steps above do nothing, hold Q, choose Dmax, and sample the brightest neutral area that has not clipped. The steps are in Inversion and sampling.

Drag the DCMY waveforms

In the inversion panel, drag either end of a waveform. The left end mainly controls the shadow baseline. The right end mainly controls gain. Move a little at a time, then look at shadows, midtones, and highlights.

Waveform Left end Right end
D Overall baseline shift Overall gain
C Red-channel shadow end Red-channel gain
M Green-channel shadow end Green-channel gain
Y Blue-channel shadow end Blue-channel gain

If the shadows are green, try lowering the left end of M a little. If the highlights are yellow and short on blue, try raising the right end of Y. After the change, check skin and midtones as well, so fixing one end does not push the other end off. The channel waveforms do not need to overlap.

Tool Use

Curves Add and drag control points. The master curve sets contrast. RGB channel curves set color

Color grading Set a color for shadows, midtones, highlights, or the whole picture, and use blend and balance for the transition
LUT Pick a preset or import a file in the LUT panel, then set its strength. Hold Z for a quick control
Local mask Add and select a mask, then adjust exposure or color inside it. Use feather for the edge

Press N to compare before and after. Press ⌘ Z to undo the latest change.

Print, scan LUTs and manual levels

Stack Print in Inversion with a scan look in the LUT panel. Choose None to disable an individual layer. Hold Z to adjust each strength. NF_C, NF_W and X5 pair with a 2383 D65 print look. Hold S to switch color modes.

chapters.title: How to remove dust from infrared and RGB film scans
chapters.description: Check whether the scan includes an infrared channel. NextFrame can use that channel to locate and repair dust. For camera scans and RGB-only files, use on-device AI detection across the frame or in a selected area. For a single speck, use the manual brush.
chapters.body:
For scattered dust in an RGB image, start with automatic dust removal. For an infrared scan or dust confined to one area, go to infrared and local AI cleaning.

Sprocket fill and borders

  1. Crop with Keep Base so the edge codes and sprocket holes you want remain.
  2. Press G to turn on sprocket fill, and hold G to adjust the threshold.
  3. Zoom in and check missed holes, edge codes, and dark parts of the picture. Lower the threshold if it fills areas it should not.
  4. Crop away the continuous white border outside the base.

Sprocket fill is white. For a motion piece with a border, choose the Border template in Live export. See Export.

Automatic dust removal

  1. Press E to open dust removal and choose Auto.
  2. RGB detection uses a local model. If the panel prompts you to download or update it, complete that step before starting detection.
  3. Click Detect dust and inspect the detected spots. Use Markers to show or hide their locations.
  4. Adjust sensitivity, or edit the dust mask with the brush and eraser. If real texture was selected, lower the sensitivity or erase that area.
  5. Click Remove and inspect the spot and the surrounding texture in the preview.
  6. Press Enter to apply, or Esc to cancel.

If this computer does not support automatic dust removal, use the Manual page. Scroll to change the brush size, then click or drag to repair dust. Hold Space and drag to pan. ⌘ Z undoes.

Infrared and local AI cleaning

For scans with an infrared channel. Press E and choose Auto. Under Infrared Dust Removal, enable Markers to see which spots the scanner channel identifies, then enable Remove to inspect the repair. Watch nearby outlines and fine lines as you adjust infrared sensitivity. This method needs no AI model. The brush and eraser edit a separate mask and leave the infrared layer intact.

For dust in one part of an RGB image. If there are specks in one corner of a sky, choose Select on the Auto tab and drag a rectangle around them. Detection starts in that region. Inspect the markers, then click Remove. For a single isolated spot you can also use the brush on the Manual tab.

How do I check that film detail survived? Compare the same area at 100%. Check both the speck and the grain, hair, or branches beside it. If real texture is marked, lower the sensitivity for the detection method you are using and inspect the markers again.

Noise reduction and sharpening

Open Detail and adjust noise reduction and sharpening near 100% view. Look at sky, skin, edges, and fine texture. Too much sharpening makes bright edges. Too much noise reduction removes grain and detail.

Glow

Open Glow and adjust strength, range, distance, and warmth. Watch the spread around highlights and the local contrast. Use the reset button on the right of the panel to return to the default.

Grain

Under Glow, open Grain and adjust:

Setting Effect
Amount Texture strength. 0 turns it off
Size How large the grain looks
Roughness The balance of fine texture and larger clumps

Start with a low amount. At 100% view, look at skin, sky, and shadows, then adjust size and roughness. A scan that already has clear film grain does not need more.

Apply to a batch

Copy settings from a reference photo. On the target, open the paste panel and check only the modules you want to sync. After a batch apply, check photos with different exposure and different subjects.

chapters.title: Batch, HDR, and LIVE export
chapters.description: Before export, choose the photos to save, then set format, size, and output.
chapters.body:
Copy settings across photos

Select several targets in the filmstrip, or press ⌘ A to select the current set. On the reference, press ⌘ C. Select the targets and press ⌘ V, then check the modules to sync in the paste panel.

Crop, Dmin, and exposure usually need their own settings on each picture. If a mask is selected, ⌘ A and similar commands act on masks. Leave mask selection before you batch-edit photos.

Keep more than one version

Press ⌘ D to make a virtual copy and compare different grades. A copy keeps its own edit settings. It becomes a separate image file only after export.

Still export

  1. Select the results and press ⌘ S to open export.
  2. Check the selected count. Choose JPEG, TIFF, or PNG.
  3. Set the long edge, quality or bit depth, and the color space.
  4. For ordinary web sharing, choose SDR and sRGB. For later editing, use a high-bit-depth format the app supports.
  5. Set the names and destination, click Export, and wait until it finishes.

Open the folder afterward and check count, size, and color. Failed items can be sent again with Retry.

HDR preview and output

In Develop, switch the Monitor to the HDR view. Drag the chart left or right to set HDR brightness, and hold the HDR preview button to see the result.

On export, set Dynamic Range to HDR and choose a strength: Auto, Natural, Standard, Strong, or Extreme. HDR currently uses Ultra HDR JPEG. Other formats are limited while HDR is on. Switch back to SDR before a Live export.

Check the file on a screen and in software that support HDR. Where HDR is not supported, you see the compatible SDR rendering. An ordinary web screenshot cannot show the full HDR brightness.

LIVE export

  1. Open export, set Dynamic Range to SDR, and choose the Live format.
  2. Choose the Signature, Border, or Full Bleed template. Turn on Show Logo if you want it.
  3. Choose the photos and destination, click Export, and wait for the short clip to finish.
  4. On macOS, NextFrame tries to save the Live Photo to Photos. You can AirDrop it to an iPhone from the library. Windows exports a Live video.

If macOS says Photos permission was not granted, the file may still be in the export folder. Grant access and write to the library again. The batch is not necessarily lost.

Format, size, and quota follow the current version and the account’s permissions.

chapters.title: Dials and waveforms
chapters.description: The dial picks a mode or adjusts a setting quickly. Waveforms control inversion directly. The common moves can happen in the preview.
chapters.body:
Hold a key to open the dial

Focus the Develop workspace, hold the key, move the pointer to an item on the dial, and finish the choice the way the interface indicates. A short press of the same key runs a different shortcut.

Hold Function
A Exposure-range presets, automatic processing
D Automatic crop mode, straighten, no crop
S Color modes, including NF_C, NF_W and X5
Q Choose Dmin or Dmax sampling
T Temperature and tint
G Sprocket-fill threshold
Z Independent print and scan LUT strengths
2, 3 Custom dials

In Processing Preferences, set the controls for Custom (2) and Custom (3). After you choose the adjustments you use often, hold the matching number key while editing.

Drag a waveform

Open the inversion panel and drag the left or right end of the D, C, M, or Y waveform. The left end controls the baseline. The right end controls gain. D adjusts the whole picture. C, M, and Y are the red, green, and blue channels.

Move a little, look at the picture, then continue. If shadows and highlights have different casts, adjust the matching end. Do not change the color only to make the waveforms overlap. More detail is in Color.

Move through the photos

Use the left and right arrow keys to change photos. N compares, V shows marks, F crops, ⌘ C / ⌘ V copy and paste settings, and ⌘ S opens export.

After a strip scan, press F to crop, choose Strip, and set every box with frame count, group count, spacing, and offset. See Strip scans.

chapters.title: Connecting an agent
chapters.description: NextFrame exposes image tools to clients that speak local MCP. Once connected, you can name a folder, a processing path, and the changes you want in conversation.
chapters.body:
Set up the connection

  1. Open NextFrame and go to Settings → Agent MCP….
  2. Add the folders the agent is allowed to process, then click Enable Local MCP.
  3. Copy the Codex or Cursor configuration shown in the window into that client’s MCP configuration.
  4. Reload the client’s tools and have the agent check that NextFrame is connected.

Use the path shown in the window on this computer. After the app quits, enable the connection again. NextFrame does not need a large-model API key.

Process a folder

You can tell the agent:

Use NextFrame to process the folder "actual/path/to/files". Keep the film base for RAW frames, and remove it for strip scans. Check the crop and color of every frame, and show the results first.

Replace the path inside the quotes. To keep editing, name the file and the change, for example “Make _200885.ARW a little brighter, and keep the current color.”

For a photo you have already adjusted by hand, say that the current settings should stay, and that the change starts from the current look.

Network

Leave cloud color correction on when the network supports it. If the color service cannot connect, say “Turn off cloud color correction for this run and continue locally.” An agent client being online does not mean NextFrame’s color service can connect.

Check and export

Look at the preview. Check crop, range, sprockets, and color. Describe the next change if you need one.

The current MCP export command opens NextFrame’s export window. You choose the format and folder and finish the export. Afterward, check the actual files in the destination.

Optional review tools

Compatible builds offer DCMY sampling, manual levels, two LUT layers, local dust repair, four-image stitching and film-border previews. Check the tool list for your connected build.

chapters.title: File formats and tethered capture
chapters.description: NextFrame can process camera copies and scans. It can also connect to a supported camera, or watch a capture folder.
chapters.body:
Import files

In the library, click Import Folder, or drop a folder onto the library area. Use Add Frames for one file or several.

Common inputs are camera RAW (for example ARW, NEF, CR2/CR3, and RAF), DNG, TIFF, and FFF. Whether a specific camera and encoding can be read is decided by the import result. Choose the single-copy path or the strip path to match the film.

Before import, check the source color space for DNG and TIFF, and the camera DCP settings, in Processing Preferences. They should match the source file. TIFF files from different scan software do not always use the same color space.

Connect a camera

  1. Connect the camera with a cable, turn it on, and choose a connection mode that allows computer control.
  2. In the NextFrame library, click Tethered Capture.
  3. Click Connect and choose a detected, supported device.
  4. Check live view. Where the controls are available, set exposure mode, shutter, ISO, white balance, quality, and size.
  5. Click the shutter button. After the photo transfers, it enters the current workflow. If import auto-processing is on, processing continues from your preferences.
  6. Disconnect when you are done.

Available controls depend on the camera and the connection. Set anything the computer cannot change on the camera body. If live view is unavailable, turn it on from the camera when the interface says so, or just take the picture. If a device cannot release the shutter remotely, use the shutter on the body.

Watch a folder

If you already have camera-control software, let it save photos to a local folder and let NextFrame pick up new files.

  1. Import that folder into NextFrame and select it.
  2. Open Tethered Capture and click Watch Folder. The current library item needs a real path on disk, and no camera should be connected.
  3. In the camera software, set the save location to the same folder.
  4. After a shot, wait for the file to finish writing, then look at the new photo and its processing result in NextFrame.
  5. Use Pause, Resume, or Close on the floating status bar to control watching.

Shoot one test file first. Confirm the save location, format, and automatic processing, then shoot the rest of the roll.

chapters.title: Troubleshooting
chapters.description: Find the symptom, then the check that goes with it.
chapters.body:
Sprocket holes missed, or the picture filled white

Press G to check the switch, and hold G to adjust the threshold. Raise it a little when holes are missed. Lower it when the picture or the edge codes are filled by mistake. Zoom in before you confirm.

Fog, low contrast, or an obvious cast

Press V and check the exposure range and Dmin. Shrink the range if it includes interfering color. If the picture has no black point, try including a little film base. You can place Dmin again on the narrow black edge or in the gap between frames. Clear it if the result gets worse. Then follow Color.

Cloud color correction fails

Check the network and the service connection. A system-wide VPN can block NextFrame’s color service. If it cannot connect, turn cloud correction off for now and keep using local inversion and hand adjustments. Turn it back on when the network returns.

A shortcut does nothing

Leave the text field or dialog and click the Develop workspace. Confirm whether a photo or a mask is selected, and tell a short press from a press-and-hold. See Keyboard shortcuts.

A feature is missing, or a button is unavailable

Check the installed version and the current mode. Some features need a camera, a device, or an account permission. HDR output, camera live view, and automatic dust removal follow the options the interface actually offers.
